The legal-retrieval review states diachronic blindness is "the one least well integrated into mainstream RAG practice" and describes exact failure modes including "the corpus may be versioned only at document granularity, producing whole-document snapshots that obscure structural-unit differentials". It also gives detection criteria: "Point-in-time recovery ... can the system return the text that was in force at T". This is direct evidence that:
- The version-selection problem at structural-unit granularity (near-duplicate clause versions) is recognized as unaddressed ("least well integrated").
- It also confirms distinction (ii) is a genuine gap (versioned only at document granularity obscures structural-unit differentials) — supports the benchmark gap.
- And it defines detection criteria (point-in-time recovery), which is essentially a version-level metric → supports distinction (i)/(ii) but also shows the metric concept is articulated (though not implemented/measured).

This supports the assessment that (i) is untested framing (the reviewer says mainstream RAG doesn't enforce it at retrieval time; "most solutions remain stronger at representation than at retrieval-time enforcement") — actually this supports the claim that post-hoc retrieval-time enforcement is under-explored. - (iii) validity/as-of (bitemporal, point-in-time) is conceptually established → pre-empted as novelty, but also confirmed as the right signal (supports M001).

input.statement: Final assessment of the three distinctions: (iii) validity/as-of semantics is conceptually pre-empted (bitemporal valid-time correctness, point-in-time resolution named as a legality-critical operation), so it cannot be a novelty claim; (ii) clause-granularity versioning is a recognized but explicitly unaddressed gap, so the benchmark is valuable while the identification of the gap is not novel; (i) retrieval-time (as opposed to representation-level) temporal enforcement is described as under-explored, which supports the rationale for a post-hoc ranking layer but remains an untested framing until measured across retrievers. The contribution therefore rests on measurement and retrieval-time enforcement, not on identifying the problem or naming the signal.

input.confidence_basis: Direct full-text evidence from a legal-retrieval review that names clause-granularity versioning as an unaddressed failure mode, states that diachronic failure is least integrated into mainstream practice, and asserts that solutions are stronger at representation than at retrieval-time enforcement; corroborated by earlier findings that the same source reports no empirical comparison.
input.resolution: Resolved: the three distinctions should not be presented as independent novelty claims. (iii) validity/as-of semantics is conceptually pre-empted - legal retrieval already requires distinguishing valid time from transaction time and names point-in-time resolution a legality-critical operation. (ii) clause-granularity versioning is a recognized but explicitly unaddressed gap ('versioned only at document granularity, producing whole-document snapshots that obscure structural-unit differentials'), so the benchmark is valuable but identifying the gap is not novel. (i) retrieval-time enforcement is described as under-explored ('most solutions remain stronger at representation than at retrieval-time enforcement'), which rationalizes a post-hoc ranking layer but is still an untested framing until measured. Consequence: the contribution must be the implementation and measurement - valid-time gating enforced at retrieval time, evaluated across base retrievers with clause-level contamination and point-in-time recovery - not the identification of the problem or the naming of the signal.

input.direction: Keep the D003 evaluation design and reframe the contribution as implementation-and-measurement rather than problem identification: enforce valid-time membership at retrieval time (post hoc, across BM25/dense/hybrid), and measure clause-level point-in-time recovery and version contamination, with answer accuracy co-primary only on answer-differential queries. Present the benchmark as filling the named clause-granularity gap, not as discovering it, and present valid-time gating as the correct signal to enforce at retrieval time rather than as a new concept.
input.hypothesis: Enforcing valid-time (as-of) membership at retrieval time, rather than only encoding time in representations, reduces clause-level point-in-time retrieval failures (returning text not in force at the query date) relative to semantic-only retrieval and to elapsed-time decay, and the reduction is larger where successive clause versions are near-duplicates and the authoritative version is not the latest.
input.rationale: The legal-retrieval review states that diachronic failure is the least well integrated into mainstream practice, that solutions are stronger at representation than at retrieval-time enforcement, and that document-granularity versioning obscures structural-unit differentials. This confirms the gap is real and explicitly recognized, while also confirming that the signal (valid-time/bitemporal) and the framing (architecture-agnostic) are not novel. The direction therefore narrows to what remains measurable and unmeasured: retrieval-time enforcement across retrievers plus clause-level point-in-time recovery metrics. It deserves investigation next because it is the smallest claim not contradicted by the retrieved evidence, it is falsifiable with existing tools, and a negative result (retrieval-time gating adds little) would itself be informative about where temporal handling belongs.
input.research_question: Does enforcing valid-time (as-of) membership at retrieval time, post hoc across sparse, dense and hybrid retrievers, improve clause-level point-in-time retrieval (returning the text in force at the query date and avoiding superseded or not-yet-in-force versions), compared with semantic-only retrieval, elapsed-time decay, and representation-level temporal handling?
